identification.summary: Nitro is the name Symantec gave in October 2011 to a series of targeted attacks that began against chemical-sector companies and used the PoisonIvy remote access Trojan delivered by spear-phishing email [S3]. Symantec judged the purpose to be industrial espionage [S3]. Palo Alto Networks (Unit 42) reported in October 2014 that a group it called Nitro was still active, using different malware (mainly Spindest, plus PCClient and Farfli variants) [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec reporting describes the same infrastructure being used against human-rights groups from about late April 2011 and the motor industry in late May 2011, before the chemical-sector wave of roughly July to mid-September 2011 [S3][S2].
identification.notes: Whether the 2014 Unit 42 'Nitro' activity involves the same operators as 2011 is a vendor linkage via infrastructure overlap, not independently verified here [S5]. Covert Grove is a pseudonym Symantec gave to an individual tied to one C2 server, not a group name [S3][S7]. Microsoft has no known Typhoon/Sleet name mapping for Nitro in the sources gathered.

attribution.confidence: Symantec stated it could not determine whether the individual it called Covert Grove was the sole attacker, had only an indirect role, or was acting on behalf of one or more other parties [S3].
attribution.basis: Symantec traced one command-and-control server to a US-hosted machine owned by a man in his 20s in Hebei province, China, whom it pseudonymized Covert Grove [S3][S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered. Sponsor left blank; the imported record's country code CN rests on this single-server finding.

objectives: Symantec assessed the goal of the chemical-industry wave as collecting intellectual property such as design documents, formulas and manufacturing processes [S3]. Trend Micro read the broader mix of chemical, human-rights, motor and defense targets as community-of-interest targeting to gather information for later, more precise attacks [S2].

regions: Press coverage of Symantec: about 48 organizations in about 20 countries, with most infected machines in the United States, Bangladesh and the United Kingdom [S3][S4]
2014: US and European organizations, plus a South Korean clothing manufacturer's website used to host malware [S6]
targeting.notes: Press accounts of Symantec's report give 29 chemical companies and 19 other firms, mostly defense [S3][S4]. Counts differ slightly across outlets. 2014 victim types come from SC Magazine's coverage of the Unit 42 report [S6].

capabilities.summary: 2011: spear-phishing emails posing as meeting invitations or security updates from business partners carried PoisonIvy, a freely available RAT; Symantec said no zero-day vulnerabilities were used and the attacks were not particularly sophisticated [S3][S4]. Trend Micro noted a human operator sits behind each PoisonIvy connection and can explore the network, steal data and install further malware, and mapped three distinct sets of C2 infrastructure from Symantec's samples, one using dynamic DNS domains [S2]. 2014: Unit 42 and SC Magazine reported mainly Spindest malware with PCClient and Farfli variants, with spear phishing and PoisonIvy absent from those cases, and compromised legitimate websites used to serve malware [S5][S6].

campaigns.name: Human-rights group targeting (same infrastructure)
campaigns.summary: Press coverage of Symantec's report says the same C2 infrastructure was used against human-rights organizations from about late April to early May 2011.

campaigns.name: Motor industry targeting
campaigns.summary: The same infrastructure was reportedly used against motor-industry targets in late May 2011.

campaigns.name: Chemical-sector wave
campaigns.summary: Spear-phishing with PoisonIvy against chemical companies from about July to mid-September 2011; Symantec counted 29 chemical firms and 19 others, mostly defense.

campaigns.name: Public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Symantec published 'The Nitro Attacks: Stealing Secrets from the Chemical Industry' (31 Oct 2011) and Trend Micro published supporting infrastructure analysis.

campaigns.name: Renewed activity reported by Unit 42
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 published new indicators (hashes, domains, IPs) for Nitro, linked through IP resolution overlap, with Spindest, PCClient and Farfli malware and victims including a US IT provider, a European office of a US geospatial imagery vendor, a European power and automation firm and a US medical imaging provider.

diamond.adversary: Unidentified operator(s); Symantec tied one C2 server to an individual in Hebei, China (pseudonym Covert Grove) but could not say if he acted alone or for others [S3].
diamond.capability: PoisonIvy RAT via spear phishing (2011); Spindest, PCClient and Farfli malware and compromised websites (2014) [S2][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Three distinct C2 sets mapped by Trend Micro including dynamic DNS domains; a US-hosted server in 2011; IP resolution overlap used by Unit 42 to link 2014 samples [S2][S3][S5].
diamond.victim: Chemical and defense firms, human-rights NGOs, motor manufacturers (2011); varied technology, power and imaging firms (2014) [S3][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial and technical intelligence; Trend Micro viewed the wider targeting as intelligence gathering for later focused attacks [S2].
diamond.technology: Email gateways and endpoints exposed to socially engineered attachments, and legitimate websites that can be compromised to host malware [S3][S6].

gaps: Symantec white paper full text could not be opened; Symantec details here come via press reports [S3].
WebFetch could not reach unit42.paloaltonetworks.com or the seebug PDF; Unit 42 details come from search-result summaries and SC Magazine coverage.
No government or vendor attribution to a sponsor; the Covert Grove link is to one server and one individual only.
Unverified whether 2014 activity is the same operators as 2011; third-party catalog (Strobes) suggests relation to APT 18 / Wekby but this was not corroborated and is not used.
No Microsoft naming, MITRE group ID or activity after 2014 found.
Dates of some press articles (SC Magazine) were not visible in search results.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Defense industrial base and chemical/manufacturing suppliers hold design data and are the relevant terrain; email gateways and employee mailboxes are the entry points [S3][S6]. STEP 2: Evidence is of a low-sophistication actor using freely available tools and no zero-days, so basic email defenses matter [S3][S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear phish with a plausible business lure, then RAT with live operator, then lateral exploration and data theft [S2][S3]; by 2014 tooling and web-based delivery changed [S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued IP collection from defense and industrial firms. MDCOA is use of compromised supplier websites and varied custom malware to reach defense-adjacent targets. Candidate indicators: PoisonIvy or Spindest-family detections, dynamic-DNS C2 domains, and IPs overlapping Unit 42 indicators [S2][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor indicator sets for Nitro across contractor reporting [S5]. (2) Authorities: defense contractor networks are owned by industry; coordination runs through the DIB reporting channels rather than direct action. (3) Mission assurance: protect design and supply-chain data at chemical and manufacturing suppliers [S3]. (4) Coordination: attribution is weak, so share indicators without asserting a sponsor [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: These attackers were the subject of an extensive report by Symantec in 2011, which termed the attackers Nitro and stated: 'The goal of the attackers appears to be to collect intellectual property such as design documents, formulas, and manufacturing processes. In addition, the same attackers appear to have a lengthy operation history including attacks on other industries and organizations. Attacks on the chemical industry are merely their latest attack wave. As part of our investigations, we were also able to identify and contact one of the attackers to try and gain insights into the motivations behind these attacks.' Palo Alto Networks reported on continued activity by the attackers in 2014.
